item.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
item.description: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects. My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing, security, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, pi

item.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
item.description: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra. The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra. Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon. This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript. The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on. I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" item.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
item.description: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io: Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README. I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML. This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite. Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem. For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers Tags: javascript, projects, python, urls, datasette, webassembly, service-workers, pyodide, datasette-lite

item.title: llm 0.37.3
item.description: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code. Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp: That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp

item.title: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0
item.description: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap, the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub.) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. I like this demo page showing both GeoJSON shapes and lat/lon points on the same map: Tags: visualization, generative-ai, datasette-lite, claude-mythos-fable, ai, llms, geospatial, openstreetmap, datasette

item.title: datasette 1.0a43
item.description: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone, which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0. A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai, Peter Olkhovets, Ilya Khalafi, and Ankita Advitot. The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { @view-transition { navigation: auto; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html:active-view-transition .content > .facet-results { view-transition-name: facet-results; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html:active-view-transition .table-wrapper:has(> table.rows-and-columns) { view-transition-name: rows-table; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) Tags: security, datasette, css, browsers, annotated-release-notes, firefox, javascript, safari, chrome

item.title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
item.description: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model '{ "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" }' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! Tags: uv, datasette-agent, llm, datasette, llms, ai, generative-ai
